readingInstruction: Read Psalm 102. It is headed “A prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the LORD.” Notice how the psalm moves from personal misery to the eternal reign of God, and how the New Testament quotes the end.
settingTheScene: Psalm 102 is one of the seven penitential psalms in church tradition. It has no named author. It is the cry of an individual who feels his life vanishing like smoke, and at the same time a prayer for Zion’s restoration, which fits the exile. It sets private suffering inside the story of God’s people and the story of creation.
observation: “Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you!” (v. 1).
“For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace” (v. 3).
“I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop” (v. 7).
“For I eat ashes like bread, and mingle tears with my drink” (vv. 9).
“My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass” (v. 11).
“But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations” (v. 12).
“You will arise and have pity on Zion; it is the time to favor her” (v. 13).
“Of old you laid the foundation of the earth… They will perish, but you will remain… but you are the same, and your years have no end” (vv. 25-27).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a rush of need: hear me, do not hide your face, answer me speedily. The description that follows is vivid and bodily. His days vanish like smoke. His bones burn. His heart is struck down like grass. He forgets to eat. He is wasted by groaning. He is like a pelican in the wilderness or an owl among ruins, a sleepless bird alone on a roof. And he feels that God has lifted him up only to throw him down. Few passages in the Bible describe depression and isolation so plainly.

The turning point is a single word at verse 12: “But you, O LORD.” Against all that is passing and fading, the psalmist sets the One who is enthroned forever. The shadow of his life lengthens, but God’s name endures to all generations. The change of view then opens his prayer outward. He asks that God will have pity on Zion. “The nations will fear the name of the LORD,” and a people yet to be created will praise him.

The psalm ends with creation itself. The heavens and earth will wear out like a garment, but God is the same. This is the final consolation for the dying and discouraged: the one in whom we trust does not change. “The children of your servants shall dwell secure.” The prayer of one man’s faintness is carried by the unchanging God.

Hebrews 1:10-12 quotes verses 25 to 27 and applies them to the Son. The one who laid the foundation of the earth and who will remain when it perishes is Jesus. So the faint and afflicted worshiper in the psalm is praying to Christ, whose years have no end.
connection: Hebrews 1:10-12 attributes Psalm 102:25-27 to the Son, showing his eternal deity. Hebrews 13:8 says, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” 2 Corinthians 4:16-18 speaks of the outer self wasting away while the inner self is renewed. Romans 8:18 says the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed. Malachi 3:6 says, “I the LORD do not change.”
application:
If you are weary or lonely, pray the first eleven verses honestly, then pray verse 12 as a turning point.

Name something that is fading in your life, and remember who remains.

Pray for the church in the places where it seems to be in ruins.
prayerPrompts: Cry out to God from your affliction.
Tell him that he is enthroned forever.
Ask him to arise and have pity.
